title: How Floods Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain how floods work, starting with a brief primer on the hydrological cycle (water cycling through evaporation, clouds, rain, rivers, and oceans, with volcanoes and the atmosphere balancing water). They cover how storms overwhelm waterways, the role of land type (forests, farmland, earthworms, clay, concrete and asphalt), seasonal monsoon flooding and the Nile, dam and levee failures (Johnstown flood of 1889, Vajont Dam, Morganza spillway, Katrina), coastal erosion and walls, why flood water is dangerous (water seeks level, cars swept away, drownings), flash floods including the 1976 Big Thompson Canyon flood in Colorado, the 1966 Florence Arno River flood and its art damage, and disease risks from floodwater. The episode opens with banter about childhood basement flooding and the 1994 Flint River flood in Albany, Georgia, and closes with a listener mail request from Adam for the Alamos Wild Lands Alliance Bird-a-thon fundraiser.

segments.title: Opening banter and childhood basement floods
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about flooding, Josh's childhood basement flooding in Toledo, and the 1994 Flint River flood in Albany, Georgia, where caskets floated out of a cemetery.

segments.title: Hydrological cycle primer
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Earth's water volume is roughly constant, with losses to the atmosphere balanced by volcanic release, and walk through evaporation, wind, cloud formation, rain, and return to the oceans.

segments.title: Storms overwhelming waterways
segments.summary: Freak storms dump more rain than rivers are shaped to hold, so water spills over banks. Rivers form over long periods and are not sized for worst-case events.

segments.title: Seasonal flooding, monsoons and the Nile
segments.summary: Common causes include large storms and snowmelt; seasonal monsoon winds bring annual flooding, and the ancient Nile's annual floods fertilized farmland, a pattern changed by dams like the Aswan Dam.

segments.title: Dam failures and the Johnstown flood
segments.summary: Dam breaks are a major flood cause. The hosts describe a Washington State dam demolition and the 1889 Johnstown flood, caused by the South Fork dam failure, with about 2,209 deaths, and mention the 1963 Vajont Dam wave.

segments.title: Land type, earthworms and levees
segments.summary: Soil and surface type determine runoff: forests and soft soil absorb water while clay, rock, concrete and asphalt do not. Tilled farmland is more prone to flooding than woodland because earthworm tunnels are lost. Levees, the Katrina breach, and the Morganza spillway opening are discussed.

segments.title: Coastlines, erosion and water seeking its level
segments.summary: Coastal walls prevent erosion but disrupt natural beach processes. Floodwater rushes because water seeks its level, so a couple of feet can sweep cars away and six inches can knock a person down; most flood deaths involve vehicles.

segments.title: Flash floods: Big Thompson Canyon 1976
segments.summary: Flash floods are the most dangerous. The July 31, 1976 Big Thompson Canyon flood in Colorado followed about twelve inches of rain in four hours, killing around 139 to 145 people during the state centennial celebration.

segments.title: Flood aftermath, Florence art damage and disease
segments.summary: Floods leave silt, mud, and sewage. The Arno River flood in Florence damaged Renaissance art and books stored in basements, and floodwater carries disease risks, so water should be boiled.

segments.title: Closing discussion and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up flood content and discuss a Nettie pot infection story, then move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Alamos Wild Lands Bird-a-thon
segments.summary: Listener Adam, research director of the Alamos Wild Lands Alliance, asks listeners to sponsor the Bird-a-thon fundraiser around Super Bird Saturday, the day before the Super Bowl, to support conservation in northwest Mexico.

segments.title: Outro and contact info
segments.summary: The hosts give contact details for listener feedback and mention the How Stuff Works app.
